description:
We're a team passionate about space exploration, technology, and interactive storytelling. Through Abandoned but Not Forgotten, we aim to bring forgotten spacecraft back to life using immersive design, interactive experiences, and real NASA data.

We believe every mission has a story worth telling, even after its final signal.
summary:
Last Signal: Project Details

Challenge: NASA Space Apps, “Abandoned but not Forgotten”
Team: Gökalp Çaycı, Uygar Yıldırım (Ankara local event)
Live site: lastsignal.earth
Repository: github.com/gokalpcayci/last-signal (public)
Type: Interactive web app, desktop and mobile
Languages: English, Turkish

Content

46 objects across three worlds: Moon (22), Mars (12), Deep Space (12)
112 NASA photos, 3D models for selected craft
Timeline from 1966 to today

Data sources

LRO LOLA elevation and albedo (Moon)
MGS MOLA elevation and TES albedo (Mars)
JPL Horizons trajectories (Deep Space)
NSSDCA, LROC, JPL, science.nasa.gov for facts and coordinates
NASA Image Library, NASA 3D Resources, NASA Trek

Technology

Vite, React 19, TypeScript, bun
three.js with React Three Fiber and drei
Custom GLSL shaders for terrain, grid, halftone and LED panels
Python scripts for map and photo processing
Vercel hosting with Web Analytics

Key features

Real-time sunlight on Moon and Mars
Scrollable timeline that time-travels the map
Globe mode with zoomable detail
Deep Space signal ping with real light travel time
Animated LED logo, Daktilo pixel font
details:
Last Signal

Last Signal is a web app made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” It shows the hardware people have left on other worlds and tells each object’s story in simple, kid-friendly language. The design looks like a real mission control screen: a dark dashboard, a lettered grid, monospace labels and LED-style displays. It’s live at lastsignal.earth and was made by Gökalp Çaycı and Uygar Yıldırım.

Three worlds

Moon. 22 objects, from the Surveyor landers to the Apollo rovers and laser mirrors, placed on real LRO elevation data. The terrain is drawn as a halftone relief lit by the real Sun, so day and night on the map match the sky today. Visitors can follow the routes the Apollo rovers drove, flood the low plains with a lava level slider, and switch between exaggerated and true-scale height.

Mars. 12 objects, including Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter. They sit on MOLA terrain, with a Mars clock based on NASA’s Mars24 method.

Deep Space. 12 probes, such as Pioneer, Voyager and New Horizons, drawn along their real paths from JPL Horizons data. The solar system appears as an LED panel. Planets sit where they really were on the chosen date. A PING button sends a light pulse to a probe and shows how long the reply takes.

Main features

A side-scrolling timeline that looks like an ASCII printout. Dragging it moves through time from 1966 to today, and the map follows along. Objects appear when they landed and turn from green to orange when they went silent.

A story panel for each object with real NASA photos, mission facts and, for some craft, a 3D model you can rotate.

A globe mode that shows the whole Moon or Mars as a sphere and adds surface detail as you zoom in.

A signal map that shows every object as one LED, plus a panel that tells you whether it is day or night at each landing site right now.

English and Turkish versions.

Layouts for phones, tablets and large screens.

Data and accuracy

Landing sites, dates and statuses were checked against NASA sources: NSSDCA, LROC, JPL and science.nasa.gov. Where NASA publishes no exact coordinates, as with Ingenuity, the app marks the location as approximate.

Technology

The app uses Vite, React and TypeScript, with three.js through React Three Fiber for the 3D scenes. Custom shaders draw the terrain, grid and halftone. Python scripts turn NASA elevation maps, albedo maps and photos into small files the browser loads quickly. The site is hosted on Vercel with Web Analytics. A 30-second launch video in both languages was recorded directly from the app by a script.

Visual identity

The logo is a mirror-symmetric inkblot shown as an animated LED matrix. It appears on the boot screen, in the navigation and as the map markers. Titles and numbers use Daktilo, a custom pixel font.
